title: National Mammography Day: Four Screening Myths That Keep Women From Getting Checked
excerpt: Most breast cancers are found in women with no family history, mammograms miss about one in five cancers, and implants are no barrier — what clinicians want women to know on October 16.
body:
• National Mammography Day falls on October 16 this year, in the middle of Breast Cancer Awareness Month — a prompt to book screening rather than wait for symptoms.
  • Around 70% of women diagnosed with breast cancer have no family history of the disease; "it doesn't run in my family" is the most dangerous myth in screening.
  • Screening mammograms still miss about 20% of breast cancers present at the time, so a lump that does not show on a mammogram still needs a workup — and dense breasts, which roughly double risk, may need ultrasound as well as mammography.
  • Implants do not rule out a mammogram, discomfort lasts seconds to minutes, and there is no fixed age to stop — the decision turns on health and life expectancy, not a birthday.

Every October, screening centres repeat the same message because the same myths keep working. National Mammography Day — the third Friday of October, October 16 this year — exists to close the gap between what women believe about breast screening and what the evidence says. These are the misconceptions clinicians say they still have to dismantle, as India Today and US screening specialists have both laid out this week.

Myth 1: "No family history, no risk"

Family history raises risk — a first-degree relative with breast cancer roughly doubles it — but the majority of cases arrive without one. Around 70% of women diagnosed have no family history or genetic link, which is why guidelines recommend screening for all women from age 40, not only those with affected relatives. Our earlier reporting found breast cancer is striking Indian women about a decade earlier than Western averages, which makes the family-history excuse especially costly for South Asian women.

Myth 2: "No pain, no problem — and a clear mammogram settles it"

Early breast cancer usually has no symptoms; that is the point of screening. The mirror-image error is over-trusting a normal result: screening mammograms miss roughly one in five cancers present at the time, according to figures cited by the National Cancer Institute, so a felt lump with a clear mammogram still goes to a physician for further workup. Women with dense breast tissue carry about twice the risk, and cancers hide more easily in dense tissue — one reason specialists may add ultrasound to mammography rather than treat either test as sufficient alone.

Myth 3: "Mammograms are unbearable, and implants make them impossible"

Compression lasts long enough to take the image and technologists minimise it; scheduling in the week after a period, when breasts are least tender, reduces discomfort further. Implants are a routine variation, not an exclusion — radiographers take additional views with the implant carefully displaced to see the tissue, as Trinity Health specialists explain. What implants and ultrasound cannot do is replace the mammogram: only mammography reliably catches the calcifications of stage 0 disease.

Myth 4: "At my age, I can stop"

There is no universal stop age. Clinicians increasingly frame the question around life expectancy — screening makes sense while a woman is healthy enough that finding a cancer early would change treatment, which for many women extends well into their 80s. The action item for this Mammography Day is concrete: if you are 40 or over and not current on screening, book it this month; if you are under 40 with a strong family history, ask about earlier, risk-based screening instead of assuming you are too young to need a plan.
